# Deployment Hardening — Planned Versus Actual

## Original recovery plan

The recovery wave intentionally froze application code and focused only on production transport. The plan required named remote phases, safe diagnostics, bounded fetch retries, repair of detached or stale branch state, exact-SHA validation, preservation of canonical activation, public verification, and a release canary.

## What was observed

Two consecutive pushes reached GitHub Actions but failed in the same opaque single SSH deployment step before the running service exposed the new reconciliation route. The product release itself had already passed 115 isolated tests and clean diff hygiene. The public Apps, Games, and Transcribe surfaces remained healthy, proving the failure was deployment-side rather than a public outage.

The original workflow bundled repository preparation, activation, and public verification into one SSH action. That made the failure phase invisible. The activation script also proved that Git checkout could advance before service restart, so the old public route alone could not tell whether fetch/reset or activation had failed.

## What was changed

Only `.github/workflows/main.yml` was rewritten in the isolated release worktree.

The deployment now has four named phases:
1. Probe production SSH reachability.
2. Prepare exact production checkout.
3. Activate canonical production server.
4. Verify canonical public release.

The checkout phase now validates the expected forty-character SHA, checks the production Git repository, retries only `git fetch` with bounded backoff, verifies `origin/main`, repairs detached or stale branch state with `checkout -B main`, cleans the checkout, and verifies a clean exact-SHA result.

A safe ERR diagnostic prints only phase, exit code, branch, HEAD, and origin/main SHA. It never enables shell tracing or prints secrets.

Activation remains delegated to the existing canonical production activation script. Public verification preserves the existing home and tunnel verifiers and adds the new reconciliation route as a deployment canary: an `INVALID_ROUTE` response proves the new Wallet router is not yet running.

## Structural outcome

The first workflow rewrite reached 132 lines and was rejected. The second reached 121 lines and was rejected. The final rewrite is 119 lines, preserving readable control flow instead of minifying it.

The application release remains unchanged. No commerce, Wallet, Apps, Games, SEO, server-runtime, or activation source was modified by this recovery wave.

## Remaining action

Commit the single validated workflow file separately, require remote-main freshness, push without force, observe the newly split GitHub Actions phases, and verify the public reconciliation canary plus primary public routes.
